questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that preventing bad data (Validation Rules, Duplicate Rules) isn't enough on its own for a governance program?
options: Prevention doesn't tell you whether it's actually working over time -- a governance program needs an ongoing, measured answer to how good the data currently is and whether that's improving
Prevention controls are unnecessary once metrics exist
Validation Rules and Duplicate Rules are deprecated Salesforce features
Metrics replace the need for any prevention controls
questions.explain: The lesson's framing is that you can't govern what you don't measure -- prevention controls need an ongoing metric to confirm they're working, not just an assumption.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a practical way to measure accuracy, given that Salesforce can't automatically verify whether a phone number or address is factually correct?
options: Accuracy cannot be measured under any circumstances
Assume all records are accurate unless a customer complains
Use the duplication rate as a direct substitute for accuracy
A sampled manual audit -- pulling a random sample of records periodically and checking them against a trusted external reference, then reporting the error rate found
questions.explain: The lesson describes sampled manual audits against a reliable external reference as the practical proxy most orgs use for accuracy, since Salesforce can't verify real-world correctness automatically.

questions.q: How does this lesson say a Duplicate Rule's "Report" action can be used, distinct from its "Alert" or "Block" actions?
options: Report disables the Matching Rule it references
Report logs potential matches for later review without disrupting the user's workflow, making it useful purely as a measurement tool on objects where Alert or Block would be too disruptive
Report automatically merges all detected duplicates
Report can only be used on the Lead object
questions.explain: A Report action gives an ongoing duplication count for metrics purposes without interrupting daily record creation, unlike Alert (which interrupts with a warning) or Block (which prevents the save).

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a declining-trend target (e.g., "below 3% and falling") for duplication rate instead of a flat 0% target?
options: Because fuzzy matching has real false-negative limits and new integration sources keep introducing fresh risk, so driving it to zero would require Block rules so aggressive they'd reject legitimate new records
Because Salesforce technically prevents duplication rate from ever being reported
Because 0% is always achievable with enough Validation Rules
Because duplication rate is not a real measurable metric
questions.explain: The lesson explains that matching has inherent limits and overly aggressive blocking causes its own problems, so a realistic governance program targets a declining trend rather than an unachievable hard zero.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens to a data-quality metric that is reported once and never revisited on a schedule?
options: It automatically becomes more accurate over time
Salesforce automatically archives it after 90 days
It is legally required to be destroyed
It becomes nearly as useless as not measuring at all, since the value of the number comes from watching it move over time and reacting to the trend
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct parallel to classification drift: a number nobody revisits on a recurring cadence quietly stops being watched, defeating the purpose of measuring it in the first place.
